prime.problem: "For each element, how many smaller ones come after it?" asks about all n² pairs. Checking them is 5 × 10⁹ tests for n = 10⁵, and inserting into a sorted list shifts almost as much. You need a way to count whole blocks of pairs at once.
prime.fits: Right after merge sort, and it reuses its merge unchanged. It also finishes insertion sort's story: the inversions insertion sort removes one swap at a time are counted here in O(n log n).
expect: count j − mid when a left item is placed
a separate count pass for Reverse Pairs
prime.goal: Explain why placing a left element during a merge reveals exactly how many smaller right elements it has, and adapt the trick to a condition like nums[i] > 2·nums[j].

attend: When a left-half element is placed, why is every right element already output smaller than it and originally to its right?
Why does every pair of positions meet in exactly one merge, so nothing is double-counted?
Why does Count Smaller sort indices instead of values?
Why can't nums[i] > 2·nums[j] be counted by the merge's own comparison, and why is a separate forward pass still linear?
When is a Fenwick tree the better tool for the same counts?

must: Left and right halves each sorted, left items earlier in the array → right items output before left item x are smaller and after it → j − mid at x's placement = its smaller-after count from this merge

Two positions are separated by exactly one merge (the level where they first join) → each pair is counted once → summing over ⌈log₂ n⌉ levels gives all inversions in O(n log n) (4 for [5, 2, 6, 1]; 11 for a)

A condition that isn't the sort order (x > 2y) → can't piggyback on the merge compare → but both halves are sorted, so the right pointer only moves forward as x grows → one extra linear count pass per merge, still O(n log n)
elevated: Counts belong to original positions → merge a list of indices keyed by value → otherwise you know how many but not whose
Strict < when pulling right items → equal values aren't counted as smaller
reference: the Fenwick rank-compression code in code/

compress.prompt: In 3–4 sentences from memory: what the merge reveals when a left element is placed, why summing it counts every inversion exactly once, and how the count pass for Reverse Pairs stays linear.
checklist: right elements already output are smaller and originally to the right
j − mid added to that left element's count
each pair of positions meets in exactly one merge
sort indices so counts land on original positions
for x > 2y, a separate forward-only pointer pass per merge
O(n log n) total; Fenwick tree is the online alternative

retrieve.q: Explain why the merge can count inversions in O(n log n) when any method that checks pairs one at a time is O(n²).
answer: at placement, one number j − mid covers a whole block of pairs at once
sortedness of both halves guarantees every one of those j pairs is an inversion
each merge is linear and there are log n levels

retrieve.q: Walk through the width-2 merge of [2, 5] + [1, 6] in Count Smaller for [5, 2, 6, 1]: in what order do items come out, what does each left item gain, and what are the final counts?
answer: 1 (right) goes first; then 2 is placed with j = 1 → +1; then 5 with j = 1 → +1; then 6 copied
the 6 on the right is bigger than everything left, so it adds nothing

retrieve.q: Elements arrive one at a time and you need "how many earlier values are larger than this one" after each arrival. Merge-count, Fenwick tree, or bisect.insort? Cost of each?
answer: merge-count needs the whole array up front: offline only
Fenwick tree over value ranks: O(log n) per arrival, but values must be compressed to ranks first
bisect.insort: O(log n) search but O(n) shift per insert, so O(n²) total

compare.q: Both count smaller-after-self in O(n log n). What does each structure store, which design choice makes one offline and the other online, and how does each fail?
answer: the merge stores nothing extra beyond the buffer; it counts during a divide-and-conquer pass over the whole array
the Fenwick tree stores prefix counts over value ranks and answers one query per element as you scan
merge fails when data streams in or changes; Fenwick fails without rank compression on wide value ranges

compare.q: Count-of-range-sums can be done by merge-counting prefix sums, while the rectangle problem keeps prefix sums in a sorted set. What question does each answer, and why does one need order-statistics per step?
answer: merge-count answers "how many pairs": a total, computed offline over all prefix sums
the sorted set answers "which earlier prefix is the best partner for this one": an argmin per step
the best-partner query needs a searchable set at each step; a count can be batched inside merges

predict.q: Run the Reverse Pairs count pass on [2, 4, 3, 5, 1]. Predict the total, and which merge (width 1, 2 or 4) finds the pairs.
predict.answer: 3. A reverse pair needs nums[i] > 2·nums[j] with i < j. Only the final 1 is small enough to be the right side: 4, 3 and 5 are all > 2·1 = 2, while 2 > 2 fails. No other pair works (4 > 2·3? no). All three are found in the width-4 merge, because the lone 1 at the end only meets the left block [2, 3, 4, 5] there; the width-1 and width-2 count passes find 0.

apply.task: Trace Count Smaller on [3, 1, 2, 0] through the width-1 and width-2 merges: for each merge write the output order and what each left element gains. Then check with brute force.
apply.done: Your counts are [3, 1, 1, 0], they sum to 5, and brute force over the 6 pairs finds the same 5 inversions.
